finalAnswer: Count the pairs whose relative order stays the same in every session.
shortExplanation: Use the first ranking to choose one direction for each pair, then reject a pair as soon as any later ranking reverses it.
detailedSteps: Store the position of each cow in every ranking. Enumerate ranks $i<j$ in the first row, so each unordered pair is considered exactly once.
Let those two cows be a and b. They already appear in that order in the first session. Check the remaining sessions: the pair contributes one if a precedes b every time, and zero otherwise.

A rejected pair cannot be consistent in the opposite direction, because its first-session order excludes that direction. Thus the passing tests count exactly the required pairs. With one cow there are no pairs; with one session every pair passes.
The position table uses $O(KN)$ space. Reading it and checking all pairs takes $O(KN^2)$ time. The answer is at most $\binom{20}{2}=190$.
keyIdeas: Fix a unique orientation before counting an unordered pair.
Compare positions, not cow identifiers or neighboring ranks.
commonMistakes: Do not count both orientations of the same pair.
A pair must keep its order in every session, not just most sessions.
alternativeMethods: For each ordered pair, count how many rows place the first cow earlier. Exactly K occurrences describe one consistent pair; the reverse direction cannot also qualify.
difficultyNotes: A small table makes the repeated comparisons direct. The first ranking prevents double counting.

finalAnswer: The first window length for which all consecutive windows are different.
shortExplanation: For each candidate length, insert all exact substrings into a fresh set. A duplicate means the observed colors could come from two different positions.
detailedSteps: Try lengths $L=1,2,\ldots,N$. For a fixed length, examine every start from $0$ through $N-L$, including the last window.

Insert each length-L substring into a set. If an insertion fails, the same observed sequence has two possible starts, so this length does not identify every location. Overlapping windows must also be compared.

If every insertion succeeds, each possible sequence identifies exactly one start. Print this length and stop. All smaller lengths have already failed, proving minimality. Length N always works because it has just one window.

Copying and comparing strings gives a conservative $O(N^3\log N)$ time bound and $O(N^2)$ stored characters. The source limit $N\le100$ makes this direct method sufficient. A one-character road returns 1; an all-equal road returns N.
keyIdeas: Uniqueness refers to starting positions, even when the windows overlap.
Trying lengths in order directly proves the first success is minimal.
commonMistakes: Reusing the set between different lengths creates unrelated collisions.
Do not omit the final start or wrap the string into a circle.
alternativeMethods: Compare each pair of suffixes character by character. If the longest shared prefix has length M, the answer is M+1: exactly those lengths at most M have a repeated window.
difficultyNotes: Exact substring comparison is enough; randomized hashing adds unnecessary collision concerns at this input size.

finalAnswer: The lexicographically first permutation satisfying every required adjacency.
shortExplanation: There are only eight cows. Enumerate their orders alphabetically and return the first one that passes every adjacency test.
detailedSteps: Sort the eight names alphabetically and start with the corresponding increasing index permutation. Read each complete constraint sentence, keeping the two endpoint names.
For each permutation, compute all eight positions. A constraint is satisfied precisely when $|\operatorname{pos}(X)-\operatorname{pos}(Y)|=1$, because either endpoint may come first.

Test every constraint. The first permutation that passes is feasible; all earlier permutations were rejected, so it is also the alphabetically earliest feasible order. The original guarantee that a solution exists ensures the enumeration succeeds.

Print all eight names on separate lines. The work is $O(8!(8+N))$ and the auxiliary storage is $O(8+N)$, where N is the number of constraints. This checks at most 40,320 orders and handles repeated constraints without changing their meaning.
keyIdeas: Enumerate a small complete search space in the required answer order.
Beside is a symmetric adjacency relation.
commonMistakes: Choosing the alphabetically first remaining cow greedily can strand a required neighbor.
A valid order is not sufficient unless every earlier alphabetical order has been excluded.
alternativeMethods: The required-adjacency graph consists of isolated vertices and path components. Orient each path in its earlier alphabetical direction, then concatenate the blocks in order of their first names. A separate proof of this block structure is needed.
difficultyNotes: Exhaustive enumeration is appropriate because eight names is a fixed, tiny domain. It makes both feasibility and alphabetical minimality explicit.
